o: Supplies brachioradialis

Brachioradialis is supplied by the radial nerve.
The musculocutaneous supplies coracobrachialis, biceps and brachialis.
Arises from the medial cord

It arises from the lateral cord (C5–7).
The medial cord gives the ulnar nerve.
Supplies the skin of the medial forearm

It ends as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
The medial forearm is supplied by the medial cutaneous nerve of forearm.
Pierces coracobrachialis

It pierces coracobrachialis, then runs between biceps and brachialis.
Its entry into the muscle is a few cm below the coracoid.
Runs in the spiral groove with the profunda brachii artery

It winds round the back of the humerus with the profunda vessels.
A midshaft fracture can damage it here.
Arises from the lateral cord

It is the larger terminal branch of the posterior cord.
The axillary nerve is the other.
Usually leaves triceps paralysed after a fracture at the spiral groove

Branches to triceps (long and medial heads) arise before the groove, in the axilla and arm.
So elbow extension is usually kept; wrist drop is the sign.
Supplies brachioradialis through the posterior interosseous nerve

Brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus are supplied by the radial nerve before it divides.
The posterior interosseous supplies most of the other extensors.
Gives branches in the arm

The ulnar nerve gives no branches in the arm.
Its first branches go to FCU and FDP near the elbow.
Supplies the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus

It supplies the parts to the ring and little fingers.
The median (anterior interosseous) supplies the lateral half.
Passes through the carpal tunnel

It passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum, in Guyon's canal beside the pisiform.
So carpal tunnel syndrome spares it.
Gets C7 fibres from the lateral cord in most people

In over 95% its C7 fibres come from the lateral cord.
These fibres supply FCU. (Last's p. 90, 124)

questions.s: In the forearm, the median nerve:
o: Supplies pronator teres

Pronator teres is the first muscle it supplies.
A lesion above the elbow loses pronation.
Supplies flexor digitorum superficialis

It supplies all of FDS.
FDS is one muscle with a single nerve supply.
Passes between the two heads of pronator teres

It enters the forearm between the humeral and ulnar heads.
It can be compressed there.
Gives a palmar cutaneous branch above the wrist

The palmar branch passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum.
So the skin of the palm is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.
Tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris

FCU inserts into the pisiform, outside the tunnel.
So does palmaris longus, superficial to the retinaculum.
Ulnar nerve

The ulnar nerve and artery pass superficial to the retinaculum.
They run in Guyon's canal.
Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve

It passes superficial to the retinaculum.
That is why palm sensation is kept in carpal tunnel syndrome.
Tendon of flexor pollicis longus

FPL runs through the tunnel in its own synovial sheath.
It is the most lateral tendon in the tunnel.
The brachial artery lies medial to the biceps tendon

The brachial artery lies just medial to the tendon.
It divides at the neck of the radius.
The median nerve lies lateral to the biceps tendon

The median nerve lies medial to the brachial artery.
Order from lateral to medial: tendon, artery, nerve.
The radial nerve lies medially in the floor

The radial nerve lies laterally, under cover of brachioradialis.
It divides there into its superficial and deep branches.
The ulnar nerve passes through the fossa

The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle.
It is outside the fossa.
Usually dislocates posteriorly

Most dislocations are anterior (subcoracoid), the head going down and forward.
The inferior capsule is the weakest part.
Has the axillary nerve at risk in dislocation

The axillary nerve winds round the surgical neck just below the capsule.
Check deltoid and regimental badge skin.
Has the long head of biceps outside the capsule

The tendon is inside the capsule, though outside the synovial membrane.
It arches over the head of the humerus.
Has a glenoid labrum that deepens the socket

The fibrocartilage labrum deepens the shallow glenoid.
The joint still relies mainly on the rotator cuff.

questions.s: The anastomosis around the scapula involves the:
o: Suprascapular artery

It reaches the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae.
It is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk.
Dorsal scapular artery

It runs down the medial border of the scapula.
It may arise from the transverse cervical or the subclavian.
Circumflex scapular artery

It is a branch of the subscapular artery from the third part of the axillary.
It passes through the triangular space.
Posterior intercostal arteries

They join the anastomosis along the medial border.
This collateral route helps when the subclavian or axillary is blocked.
The cords are named by their relation to the first part of the axillary artery

They are named by their relation to the second part, behind pectoralis minor.
There they lie lateral, medial and posterior.
The medial cord gives the musculocutaneous nerve

The musculocutaneous comes from the lateral cord.
The medial cord gives the ulnar nerve.
The posterior cord gives the long thoracic nerve

The long thoracic arises from the roots (C5–7).
The posterior cord gives the subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial nerves.
Both the lateral and medial cords contribute to the median nerve

Lateral and medial roots join in front of the axillary artery.
Its fibres are C(5)6–T1.

questions.s: Concerning the intrinsic muscles of the hand:
o: Palmar interossei adduct the fingers towards the middle finger

PAD: palmar adduct; DAB: dorsal abduct.
Both are supplied by the deep ulnar nerve.
All the lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve

The median supplies the lateral two; the ulnar supplies the medial two.
The pattern follows FDP.
The dorsal interossei are supplied by the median nerve

They are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
Loss causes guttering between the metacarpals.
Adductor pollicis is supplied by the median nerve

Adductor pollicis is supplied by the ulnar nerve.
Its loss gives Froment's sign.
